questions.q: In a simply supported beam, why is the rebar placed at the bottom, and what is the primary role of the concrete at the top?
o: The placement is purely for ease of construction.
Rebar is at the bottom to resist compression; concrete at the top resists tension.
Rebar handles the tensile stresses at the bottom; concrete at the top resists compressive stresses.
Concrete handles tensile stresses at the top; rebar handles squeezing at the bottom.
questions.n: Concrete is strong in compression but weak in tension. In a simply supported beam, the bottom stretches (tension) and the top squeezes (compression).

questions.q: Why is concrete considered the 'perfect' partner for steel rebar in terms of temperature behavior?
o: They have almost the identical Coefficient of Thermal Expansion.
Steel becomes stronger when heated by the concrete's hydration.
They chemically merge into a new alloy.
Concrete is a natural insulator for steel.
questions.n: Because they expand and contract at nearly the same rate, they don't tear away from each other during temperature changes.

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of the 'Deformations' (ribs) found on the surface of steel rebars?
o: To indicate the grade of the steel.
To prevent the rebar from rusting.
To provide mechanical interlock and increase bond surface area.
To make the rebar look more professional.
questions.n: Ribs ensure that the steel and concrete 'grip' each other tightly, forcing them to act as a single composite unit.

questions.q: In a cantilever balcony slab, where should the primary tension reinforcement (rebar) be placed, and why?
o: Cantilevers do not require rebar.
At the bottom, because all beams have rebar at the bottom.
At the top, because the 'stretching' (tension) occurs at the top of the member.
In the middle to stay neutral.
questions.n: In a cantilever, the beam bends downward, causing the top fibers to stretch and the bottom fibers to compress.

questions.q: Why is the high alkalinity of concrete (pH 12-13) beneficial for the embedded rebar?
o: It helps the concrete dry faster.
It creates a passivation layer that protects the steel from corrosion.
It makes the concrete easier to pour.
It increases the weight of the member.
questions.n: The alkaline environment prevents the oxidation of steel, essentially acting as a chemical shield against rust.

questions.q: What is the standard concrete cover for structural members permanently exposed to earth (like footings), and why is it thicker than for a column?
o: 40 mm; for ease of pouring.
75 mm; to protect against moisture and chemicals in the soil.
20 mm; soil is a natural protectant.
100 mm; to prevent the building from sinking.
questions.n: Soil contains sulfates and moisture that can penetrate concrete; 75mm ensures the rebar remains isolated from these corrosive elements.

questions.q: During inspection, you notice rebars are touching the plywood forms. What is the immediate risk if you proceed with the pour?
o: The concrete will set too quickly.
Nothing, it's a common site practice.
The building will be too heavy.
Honeycombing and immediate exposure leading to rebar corrosion.
questions.n: If rebar touches the form, there is zero concrete cover. The steel will be exposed to air/moisture, causing it to rust and weaken the structure.

questions.q: When can side forms (non-load bearing) of a beam be removed compared to the bottom 'soffit' forms?
o: Only after the owner pays the bill.
Side forms: 24–48 hours; Soffit forms: 14–21 days.
Both can be removed after 24 hours.
Side forms: 14 days; Soffit forms: 48 hours.
questions.n: Side forms just hold the shape; soffit forms carry the weight until the concrete gains enough strength to be self-supporting.

questions.q: Why is it common practice to 'wet' wooden formworks before pouring concrete?
o: To prevent the dry wood from absorbing the mixing water from the concrete.
To cool the site down.
To clean the dust off the wood.
To make the wood expand and tighten the joints.
questions.n: Dry wood acts as a sponge; if it sucks out the water needed for hydration, the concrete surface will be weak and crumbly.

questions.q: What is the purpose of 'Form Oil' or a release agent?
o: To prevent the concrete from bonding to the formwork for a clean strip.
To waterproof the concrete.
To keep the rebar in place.
To make the concrete shine.
questions.n: Without it, the concrete sticks to the forms, causing surface damage (spalling) when the forms are removed.

questions.q: Is concrete curing primarily done to 'cool down' the concrete member?
o: Only if the concrete is poured at night.
No, it is to maintain moisture for the chemical reaction of hydration.
Yes, to prevent the rebar from melting.
Yes, hydration produces high heat that must be quenched.
questions.n: Hydration is the chemical process that creates strength. If water evaporates too early, the process stops, and the concrete never reaches its design strength.

questions.q: What is the 'Critical Period' for curing concrete to achieve its maximum potential strength?
o: The first 24 hours.
After the roof is installed.
Between day 14 and day 28.
The first 7 days.
questions.n: Most hydration occurs early; 70% of strength is typically achieved in the first week if moisture is maintained.

questions.q: What structural defect occurs if you pour concrete in extreme heat without proper curing?
o: Plastic Shrinkage Cracks (Map Cracking).
The concrete will turn back into dust.
Nothing, heat actually helps concrete dry.
The rebar will expand and break the concrete.
questions.n: When the surface dries too fast relative to the interior, it shrinks and tears, creating a network of shallow cracks.

questions.q: Why is 'Curing by Ponding' considered highly effective for horizontal slabs?
o: It makes the slab waterproof automatically.
It allows workers to wash their tools in the slab.
It saves on water costs.
It ensures 100% saturation and uniform temperature distribution.
questions.n: Ponding creates a total barrier against evaporation and prevents thermal gradients that can cause cracking.

questions.q: Can you 'over-cure' concrete to its detriment?
o: Only if the water contains salt.
Yes, too much water makes the concrete soft.
Yes, it will cause the rebar to dissolve.
No, theoretically longer curing leads to higher strength and durability.
questions.n: Hydration can continue for years as long as moisture is present, constantly refining the pore structure and increasing density.

questions.q: In a monolithic pour, how do the slab and the beam work together structurally?
o: The beam carries 100% of the load without slab help.
The slab just sits on top like a lid.
They act as independent members.
They act as a T-Beam, where the slab serves as the 'flange'.
questions.n: The top part of the slab helps the beam resist compression, making the entire system much more efficient.

questions.q: Where is the 'Critical Section' for shear in a beam relative to the face of the supporting column?
o: Inside the column itself.
At a distance 'd' (effective depth) from the face of the support.
Shear is uniform across the whole beam.
At the exact center of the beam.
questions.n: Code specifies this distance because diagonal shear cracks usually initiate at this specific point due to stress concentrations.

questions.q: Why are beams typically designed to be deeper than they are wide?
o: To hide the electrical conduits better.
To make them easier to fit between walls.
Because depth significantly increases the Moment of Inertia and resistance to bending.
Wide beams are illegal in the Philippines.
questions.n: Bending resistance is proportional to the square (or cube) of the depth; doubling depth is far more effective than doubling width.

questions.q: In a 'Two-Way Slab' (aspect ratio less than 2), how is the load distributed to the beams?
o: The load stays in the center of the slab.
Load goes only to the columns.
Load goes only to the two shorter beams.
Load is distributed in four directions (trapezoidal and triangular patterns).
questions.n: Because the slab is nearly square, it bends in both directions, transferring load to all four supporting beams.

questions.q: What is the primary function of 'Stirrups' in a beam?
o: To resist diagonal tension (shear stresses).
To increase the compressive strength of the concrete.
To make the beam fireproof.
To hold the main bars together during the pour.
questions.n: Beams tend to tear diagonally near supports; stirrups 'stitch' these potential cracks together.

questions.q: A worker adds excessive water to the concrete mix to make it 'easier to pour.' What is the definite structural result?
o: Higher Strength because of more water for hydration.
Lower Strength; higher water-cement ratio creates more voids and pores.
The concrete becomes more flexible.
Better finish quality.
questions.n: Strength is inversely proportional to the W/C ratio. Excess water that doesn't react leaves behind holes, weakening the member.

questions.q: What property of concrete is the 'Slump Test' actually measuring at the job site?
o: Chemical composition of the cement.
Consistency and Workability.
Final Compressive Strength.
The temperature of the mix.
questions.n: It ensures the concrete has the right 'flow' to fill the forms without being too liquid (weak) or too dry (honeycombing).

questions.q: Why is 'Vibration' necessary during a pour, and what is the danger of 'Over-vibration'?
o: Vibration removes trapped air; over-vibration causes segregation of aggregates.
Vibration mixes the cement; over-vibration dries it out.
Vibration is only for aesthetic purposes.
Vibration makes the rebar hot; over-vibration melts the forms.
questions.n: Proper vibration eliminates voids; too much causes heavy stones to sink and water/paste to rise, creating a non-uniform member.

questions.q: If a 'Cold Joint' occurs because a concrete truck was delayed, what must be done to ensure a structural bond?
o: Demolish the entire beam immediately.
Add more water to the new concrete.
Just pour the new concrete on top of the old.
Clean and roughen the surface, and use a bonding agent.
questions.n: You must remove the 'laitance' and create a mechanical and chemical bridge for the new pour to stick to the hardened concrete.

questions.q: What is the '28-Day Cylinder Test' in structural engineering?
o: A test for the waterproof quality of the slab.
A test to see if the building will stand for 28 years.
A check for the placement of the electrical conduits.
The industry standard to confirm the concrete reached its Design Strength (f'c).
questions.n: 28 days is the benchmark where concrete is assumed to have reached its near-full strength for legal and structural acceptance.
